title: Old-time players freely asked each other questions
summary: Guesnon says the old men shared knowledge of chords freely, unlike today's players, and names banjoists he learned from.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: There's another thing I remember you've talked about, which we never did get on tape, that you're not ashamed to ask people questions to show you something. Whereas some musicians will try to act like they know it all already, and they're ashamed, you know, to ask somebody to show them anything. But you say, in the old days, you'd get together and you'd watch somebody and show me how to do that.

Well, you see, Bill, those days, that was the basic conception of music. Because you take all the great players around you, let's put it to that. Because, in fact, there was no such a thing as a great New Orleans musician. There was no such a thing. Some guys knew music. Some guys could read pretty well. But you couldn't put them in the class of a master musician. They were master players. In other words, they're dependent on learning the basic fundamentals of their instrument first. Know your instrument. That was the theme of the old man. Know your instrument. In other words, the music is good in its place. We can fight with that. We can wrestle with the music, play it, spell it. But once we get it in our head, how it go, the power we put behind it is the thing that's going to count. And the older man always was like that. You see, today, a guy figures that it makes him inferior to come to you and ask you what chord. He would rather sit down all night and make the wrong chord. But here's a good one like that. You take Manuel Sales, Danny Barker, myself, Poissy Sevier, Hendrick Kimball. All them men I'm telling you about were all good banjo players. And all of us got a knowledge of learning from each other. Say, man, what chord that was. Let me see how you done that. Or so and so. Well, look, I was playing the number last night and went to the bridge. What chord was in the bridge? E-7 or A minor. Well, that's it. Okay, man. But that way you knew. And you were going to go sit in a man's band. You wasn't going to cut no hog. But the other, the guy today, he just figured if he asks you, that makes you know, it's something to be ashamed of. That's why around your ring, you only got nobody left to play.
